description: Ictal Neurolite brain perfusion SPECT study was performed. CLINICAL INTERPRETATION: This is an abnormal computer-assisted prolonged video EEG monitoring session due to frequent focal epileptiform discharges over the right frontal and right frontopolar head regions. In addition, frequent bisynchronous atypical spike and wave, maximal over to the right, were present, and at times in trains of 3 Hz lasting up to 8-10 seconds without clinical accompaniment. During sleep, there was increased activation of these epileptiform discharges. During the recording, the patient had five of his typical partial seizures, one of which had no definite EEG correlate, two of indeterminate onset, and two of right frontal onset. These findings are consistent with a localization-related epilepsy with a probable right frontal or right frontotemporal onset. An ictal SPECT injection was performed during one of the patient's typical right frontal onset seizures. 

EEG CLASSIFICATION: Special study - computer-assisted prolonged video EEG; Dysrhythmia gr. 3 right frontal spike and wave and sharp waves, right frontal paroxysmal fast activity, and bisynchronous atypical spike and sharp waves, maximal right; Sleep - increased activation; Recorded one of the patient's typical partial seizures with no definite EEG correlate; Recorded two of the patient's typical partial seizures of indeterminate onset; Recorded two of the patient's typical partial seizures of probable right frontal onset; Ictal SPECT injection; EKG monitor. 

REPORT: Computer-assisted prolonged video EEG monitoring was performed for approximately 9 days. 

BACKGROUND: The wake recording revealed 9-10 Hz alpha activity over the posterior head regions. There is intermittent right frontal theta slowing. The sleep recording contained normal symmetric activity, including spindles, V-waves, and K-complexes. 

INTERICTAL DISCHARGES: During the wake recording, the patient had frequent spike and wave and sharp waves over the right frontal head region, which were at times almost continuous without clinical correlate (Fp2, F4). In addition, there were busts of paroxysmal fast activities over the right frontal head region (F4). There were also bisynchronous atypical spike and wave activity, maximal right, at times in trains of 3 Hz without clinical accompaniment. During drowsiness and sleep, there was increased activation of these discharges. 

CLINICAL EVENTS: During the monitoring session, the patient had five of his typical clinical events occurring out of wakefulness. All of these events were stereotypic, characterized by behavioral arrest, decreased responsiveness to questioning, and postictal amnesia of the events.Event #1 The mother reported that the patient appeared unfocused. There was no definite EEG correlate Seizure #2 Clinically, the patient was watching TV with his head already turned to the right and eating prior to EEG change. There was subtle decrease promptness to questioning. At 19:02:50, there was a brief right shoulder jerk. The EEG showed chewing artifact prior to clinical onset, at which time there was concomitant rhythmic theta activity over the right temporal (T10), which spread over to the right frontal (F4) about 10 seconds later, and to the right posterotemporal head region. The rhythmic activity evolves into a right frontal spike and wave activity at 19:02:39. Postictally, at 19::03:13, there was a brief left leg jerk. Seizure #3 Clinically, the patient was having lunch, alerted his mother when she called but did not answer further questions during the electrographic EEG change. He also did not recall the memory phrase. The EEG prior to clinical onset showed chewing artifact. At 13:50:41, there was semirhythmic rhythmic activity over the right temporal in a theta frequency (T8, T10), which then involved the right frontal and right temporal regions (Fp2, F4, F8, F10). The rhythmic activity then evolved into a delta activity at 13:51:16 until 13:51:23.Seizure #4 At 18:18:01, the EEG showed a low amplitude fast activity over the right frontal head region (F4), then a generalized attenuation followed by right frontal delta. At 18:18:10, the rhythmic delta activity involves the right temporal region (P8,T10), which evolves into a theta activity, with reflected rhythm over the left temporal region. Clinically, there was a brief non-forced head turn to the right at 18:18:07. At 18:18:33, there were unsteadiness of the hand, and when questioned, he was poorly responsive and answered yes or nods. Seizure # 5 at 12:13:33 to 12:14:40, with ictal injection at 12:13:58. The EEG showed a sentinel bifrontal spike and wave activity, maximal over the right frontopolar, followed by generalized attenuation, which evolves into a rhythmic theta activity emerges over the right parietal and midline central head regions about six seconds later. Delta frequency activity then emerges and spread over to the right frontocentral head region, and then theta frequency activity settling over the right temporal region. The ictal injection performed during the temporal phase of the EEG change. Clinically, there were a few subtle non-forced head turn to right, and he was unresponsive to questioning, does not talk, and post-ictally was amnestic of the event. The EKG monitor was unremarkable.

EEG CLASSIFICATION: Special study - intraoperative recording for intracranial electrode implantation of right 6x8 frontal grid (RFG); 4x6 right temporal grid (RTG); 4x6 right parietal grid (RPG); 4-contact straight strip at the right anterior temporal region (RAT); 4-contact straight strip at the right posterotemporal region (RPT); and 4-contact right temporal depth (RTD) electrode.

REPORT: Intracranial electrode implantation was performed as follows: a 6x8 grid was inserted over the right frontal region with contact #1 oriented inferiorly and anteriorly (RFG-right frontal grid). A 4x6 grid was inserted over the right temporal lobe with contact #1 oriented inferiorly and anteriorly (RTG-right temporal grid). A 4x6 grid was placed over the right parietal region with contact #1 oriented superiorly and posteriorly (RPG-right parietal grid). A 4-contact straight strip was inserted so that the strip wrapped beneath the right anterior temporal lobe with contact #4 oriented superiorly (RAT-right anterior temporal). A 4-contact straight strip was wrapped beneath the right posterotemporal lobe with contact #4 oriented superiorly (RPT-right posterotemporal). A 4-contact orthogonal depth electrode was inserted in the anterior temporal region (between contacts #2 and #8 of RTG), with the tip being contact #1 approaching the amygdala (RTD-right temporal depth). Regions of special interest for this recording include F4, which is located approximately at the site of contact #27 on RFG. Also of interest is Fp2, which is approximately at the site of contact #33 on RFG.Recordings from all the contacts were satisfactory.

CLINICAL INTERPRETATION: This is an abnormal computer-assisted prolonged intracranial video EEG monitoring session due to the presence of frequent independent right frontal, right parietal and right temporal epileptiform discharges. During the monitioring session, the patient had total of eleven seizures, including two seizures, which were subclinical. The first six seizures showed a diffuse ictal onset over the right frontal and right temporal grids. The last five seizures showed either a focal ictal onset simultaneouslyfrom the right anterior temporal strip (RAT#2) and the posterior superior region of the right frontal grid (RFG #44-48), or focal onset from these two foci independently. These findings could be consistent with a localization-related epilepsy with seizure onset in the right frontotemporal neocortex. 

EEG CLASSIFICATION: Special study - computer-assisted prolonged intracranial video EEG; Dysrhythmia gr. 3 independent right frontal, right temporal, and right parietal spike and sharp waves; Recorded six partial seizure of diffuse right frontotemporal onset; Recorded five partial seizures of focal right frontotemporal, right temporal, and right frontal onset; EKG monitor. 

REPORT: Computer-assisted prolonged intracranial video EEG monitoring was performed for approximately 7 days. A 6x8 grid was inserted over the right frontal region with contact #1 oriented inferiorly and anteriorly (RFG-right frontal grid). A 4x6 grid was inserted over the right temporal lobe with contact #1 oriented inferiorly and anteriorly (RTG-right temporal grid). A 4x6 grid was placed over the right parietal region with contact #1 oriented superiorly and posteriorly (RPG-right parietal grid). A 4-contact straight strip was inserted so that the strip wrapped beneath the right anterior temporal lobe with contact #4 oriented superiorly (RAT-right anterior temporal). A 4-contact straight strip was wrapped beneath the right posterotemporal lobe with contact #4 oriented superiorly (RPT-right posterotemporal). A 4-contact orthogonal depth electrode was inserted in the anterior temporal region (between contacts #2 and #8 of RTG), with the tip being contact #1 approaching the amygdala (RTD-right temporal depth). Regions of special interest for this recording include F4, which is located approximately at the site of contact #27 on RFG. Also of interest is Fp2, which is approximately at the site of contact #33 on RFG. 

INTERICTAL DISCHARGES: During the wake and sleep recording, there was initial diffuse epileptiform discharge over the right frontotemporal grid. By postoperative day 3, there were increased activation of independent right parietal and right temporal discharges. There were rare epileptiform discharges from the right mesial temporal depth electrode. The most frequent activation was over the right frontal grid in electrode #28-32, 35, 37-41, 44-48, 1, 2, 9-12, and 14. In addition, paroxysmal fast activity were present in RFG #1, 9, 10, 41, 28, 29; and RTG #19 and 20.

The date and time of the subclinical seizure #1 00:44:12 to 00:45:11. The EEG showed at onset a generalized diffuse attenuation over the right frontal and right temporal grids, with paroxysmal fast activity RFG #41, 42, and 43. At about 10 seconds ictal onset, there was rhythmic alpha activity in RAT #2-3 with subsequent spread to RTG #3 in rhythmic slow wave activity in RTG #1-2, RTG #7-12, and RTG #2-4.Seizure #2 occurred at 03:01:28 to 03:02:47. Clinically, he aroused from sleep, looks to the right, and stared. The EEG showed generalized attenuation over the right frontal and right temporal grids. Paroxysmal fast activity was present in RFG contacts #41, 43, and 44. At about 3-4 seconds after ictal onset, there was rhythmic alpha activity at RAT #2 which then spread to the RTD #1, settling in the right temporal grid and right mesial temporal depth electrode. The seizure offset occurred in the mesial temporal depth electrodes before in the right lateral temporal grid. The EEG showed diffuse attenuation with fast activity in RFG contacts #46, 47, and 48 and RFG #30-32. There was then rhythmic alpha activity over right anterior temporal RAT #2-4 and RPT #1-3. The electrographic seizures settles over the right temporal grid when the patient was symptomatic. Seizure #5 occurred at 05:03:45 to 05:03:06. The EEG showed generalized attenuation and paroxysmal fast activity in RTG contacts #22 and 23 followed by paroxysmal fast activity in RFG #31-32. When the patient was symptomatic and staring to the right, there was rhythmic alpha activity in RAT #2 which subsequently involves RTG contacts #2-4, and 10, RAT #1-4, RPT #1-4, and RTD #1.Seizure #7 occurred at 01:04:00 to 01:04:59. The EEG showed rhythmic alpha activity in RAT #2.Seizure #10 was a subclinical seizure at 17:38:46 to 17:39:29.Seizure #11 occurred at 04:55:05 to 04:56:27. The EEG showed alpha activity in RFG #44-48 before rhythmic alpha activity in RAT #2 at 04:55:15, with subsequent spread at 04:55:30 to the right temporal grid and RTD #1.In addition, there were four clinical events identified by parents characterized by brief slow to responsiveness, which had no abnormal EEG change. description: After induction of general anesthesia, the patient was placed in Mayfield pinions set to 60 pounds of pressure. The incision was marked and then prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. After pausing for correct patient, procedure, and site, the incision was infiltrated with diluted bupivacaine andepinephrine. Incision was then made with a 15 blade just scoring the skin. The incision was extended down through the scalp to the bone using a needle-point cautery. The scalp flap was reflected anteriorly as one with the temporalis muscle underneath and secured in place with fish hooks and towel clips. Next using a Midas drill with a pediatric perforator bit, burr holes were placed just above the zygoma, in the keyhole, at the posterior aspect of the incision in the frontoparietal region, and superiorly just lateral to the sagittal sinus. The bone flap was then turned with a footplate and B5 bit. After the bone flap was elevated, no dural tears were seen. The dura was then opened using a 15 blade and then a Jones scissors; this also was reflected anteriorly with the scalp flap. After the dura was opened, Photography was called to take a picture of the exposure in a fixed position. Following this with the assistance of the neurology team, subdural grid electrodes were placed. First, two 1 x 4 strips were placed in the subtemporal region. Next, another grid was place covering the temporal region. Second, another grid was placed overlying the frontal region. Finally, a grid was placed overlying the parietal region. Each of these grids was secured in place with a 3-0 Vicryl stitch. Once again, Photography was called, and the position of these grids was documented. Each of the grid leads was then externalized through the scalp using a 14-gauge needle and angiocatheter and was hooked up to EEG monitoring. After confirmation that all the grids were functioning properly, the durawas then closed with interrupted 2-0 Vicryl sutures. The wound was thenc opiously irrigated with bacitracin irrigation. Following closure of the dura, the bone flap was then replaced with temporary 2-0 silk stay sutures. The subgaleal layer was then closed using 2-0 Vicryl suture. Finally, the skin was closed using staples. Each of the grid leads that had been externalized was then sutured to the skin using a 3-0 silk in a pursestring stitch. The patient was then taken out of his Mayfield pinions, and a sterile head wrap was placed. He was then taken while intubated directly to CT scan for final confirmation of grid location with the spiral CT scan. The patient was then taken to the PACU intubated where he was to proceed to extubation.
